title: Metallurgy
tagline: Learn how metals are extracted, refined and protected based on their reactivity.

overview.intro: Metallurgy deals with the occurrence of metals and the processes used to extract, refine and utilise them. The choice of extraction method depends largely on the metal’s position in the activity series and the nature of its ore. This chapter covers common terms such as ore, gangue and flux, concentration of ores, roasting and calcination, reduction methods, refining, and alloys, with emphasis on principles rather than industrial detail beyond syllabus scope.

learn.title: Occurrence of Metals and Basic Terms

blocks.text: Metals occur in the earth’s crust either in free (native) state or in combined state as minerals. Minerals that contain a sufficiently high percentage of metal and from which the metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently are called ores. Unwanted earthy impurities associated with ores, such as sand and clay, are known as gangue or matrix.

During extraction, a flux may be added to combine with gangue and form a fusible substance called slag, which can be removed easily. Understanding these terms helps in describing each stage of metallurgy clearly and distinguishing between similar-sounding concepts.

items.meaning: A naturally occurring compound or element found in the earth’s crust.
A mineral from which a metal can be extracted economically.
Earthy impurities present in an ore.
A substance added to combine with gangue to form slag.

learn.title: Concentration of Ore and Conversion to Oxide

blocks.text: Concentration (dressing) of ore removes gangue and increases the proportion of metal compound. Methods depend on physical or chemical properties: hydraulic washing for dense ores, froth flotation for sulphide ores, and magnetic separation when either ore or gangue is magnetic. The chosen method improves efficiency of subsequent extraction steps.

Concentrated ores are often converted to oxides because oxides are easier to reduce. Roasting involves heating sulphide ores strongly in presence of excess air to form oxides and release sulphur dioxide, while calcination involves heating carbonate or hydrated ores in limited or no air to remove volatile impurities and produce oxides.

items.note: Sulphide ore converted to oxide in excess air.
Carbonate ore decomposed in limited air.

learn.title: Reduction and Extraction Based on Activity Series

blocks.text: The method of reducing a metal compound to the metal depends on the metal’s reactivity. Highly reactive metals such as sodium, calcium and aluminium form very stable compounds and are extracted by electrolytic reduction of their molten salts or oxides. Moderately reactive metals such as zinc and iron are commonly obtained by reducing their oxides with carbon or carbon monoxide.

Less reactive metals such as copper and mercury can be obtained by heating their compounds alone or by simple reduction, and very unreactive metals like gold may occur native. The activity series thus provides a guide: the higher the metal, the more difficult it is to reduce its compounds by chemical reducing agents.

blocks.caption: Reactivity and extraction approach
rows: Oxides/salts too stable for carbon reduction
Oxides can be reduced on heating
Compounds less stable; some occur native

blocks.text: Metals obtained after reduction often contain impurities and require refining. Methods include electrolytic refining, distillation for volatile metals, and liquation for metals with low melting points. Electrolytic refining, such as for copper, produces high-purity metal by transferring it from an impure anode to a pure cathode.

Alloys are homogeneous mixtures of two or more metals, or a metal with a non-metal, prepared to enhance properties such as strength, hardness, resistance to corrosion or melting behaviour. Examples include brass (copper and zinc), bronze (copper and tin) and steel (iron with carbon and other elements). Alloying tailors materials for specific uses.

items: Refining improves electrical conductivity and mechanical properties of metals.
Alloys are usually stronger or more corrosion-resistant than pure metals.
Composition of an alloy is chosen according to desired application.

blocks.text: Corrosion is the gradual deterioration of a metal due to chemical reactions with substances in the environment, such as oxygen and moisture. Rusting of iron is a common example requiring both air and water. Corrosion weakens structures and causes economic loss, making prevention important.

Prevention methods include painting, greasing or oiling, galvanisation (coating with zinc), electroplating and alloying. These methods either isolate the metal from the environment or provide sacrificial protection. Choice of method depends on the object’s use and exposure conditions.

items.text: Galvanised iron sheets resist rusting due to a protective zinc coating.
items.note: Zinc acts as a barrier and can provide sacrificial protection.

items.text: Stainless steel resists corrosion better than ordinary iron due to alloy composition.
items.note: Alloying improves resistance to environmental attack.

keyPoints: Ores are minerals from which metals can be extracted economically; gangue is unwanted impurity.
Concentration methods include hydraulic washing, froth flotation and magnetic separation.
Roasting heats sulphide ores in excess air; calcination heats carbonate ores in limited air.
Extraction method depends on metal reactivity: electrolysis for highly reactive metals, carbon reduction for moderately reactive ones.
Refining produces purer metals suitable for use; electrolytic refining is common for copper.
Alloys are mixtures designed to improve strength, hardness or corrosion resistance.
Corrosion is environmental deterioration of metals; rusting of iron needs air and moisture.
Prevention includes coating, galvanisation, electroplating and alloying.
Flux combines with gangue to form removable slag.
Balanced equations and correct process names are important in metallurgy answers.

Heating an ore in limited or no air, commonly used for carbonate ores.

questions.prompt: The earthy impurities present in an ore are called:
questions.answer: gangue
questions.explanation: Gangue refers to unwanted impurities like sand and clay associated with ores.
questions.commonMistake: Slag is formed when flux combines with gangue, not the original impurity.

questions.prompt: Roasting is carried out by heating the ore:
questions.answer: in excess of air
questions.explanation: Roasting converts sulphide ores to oxides by heating strongly in excess air.
questions.commonMistake: Calcination is done in limited or no air.

questions.prompt: Highly reactive metals are generally extracted by:
questions.answer: electrolysis of molten compounds
questions.explanation: Their compounds are very stable and cannot be reduced easily by common chemical reducing agents.
questions.commonMistake: Carbon reduction is suitable for many moderately reactive metals, not highly reactive ones.

questions.prompt: Froth flotation is most suitable for concentration of:
questions.answer: sulphide ores
questions.explanation: In froth flotation, sulphide ore particles preferentially attach to froth and are separated.
questions.commonMistake: Choose concentration method based on ore properties.

questions.prompt: Brass is an alloy of:
questions.answer: copper and zinc
questions.explanation: Brass is made by combining copper with zinc to improve properties.
questions.commonMistake: Copper and tin form bronze, not brass.

questions.prompt: Calcination is commonly used for:
questions.answer: carbonate ores
questions.explanation: Heating carbonate ores in limited air drives off carbon dioxide and forms oxides.
questions.commonMistake: Sulphide ores are usually roasted in excess air.

questions.prompt: The purpose of adding flux during smelting is to:
questions.answer: form slag with gangue
questions.explanation: Flux reacts with gangue to produce a fusible slag that can be removed.
questions.commonMistake: Flux removes impurities; it does not create them.

questions.prompt: Which metal is most likely to be found in the native state?
questions.answer: Gold
questions.explanation: Very unreactive metals resist corrosion and may occur naturally in native form.
questions.commonMistake: Highly reactive metals are found only in combined state.

questions.prompt: A homogeneous mixture of two or more metals is called an ________.
questions.answer: alloy
questions.explanation: Alloys are prepared to obtain improved or desired properties.
questions.commonMistake: An ore is a naturally occurring mineral, not a prepared mixture.

questions.prompt: The fusible mass formed by combination of flux and gangue is called ________.
questions.answer: slag
questions.explanation: Slag separates from molten metal and can be removed easily.
questions.commonMistake: Do not confuse slag with flux or gangue.

questions.prompt: Coating iron with zinc to prevent rusting is known as ________.
questions.answer: galvanisation
questions.explanation: Galvanisation protects iron by providing a zinc layer.
questions.commonMistake: Electroplating uses electrolysis; galvanisation specifically refers to zinc coating.

questions.prompt: Differentiate between a mineral and an ore.
questions.answer: A mineral is any naturally occurring element or compound in the earth’s crust. An ore is a mineral from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently.
questions.explanation: All ores are minerals, but not all minerals are ores.
questions.commonMistake: Include the idea of economic extraction when defining ore.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between roasting and calcination?
questions.answer: Roasting is heating an ore strongly in excess air, usually to convert sulphide ores to oxides. Calcination is heating an ore in limited or no air, usually to convert carbonate or hydrated ores to oxides by removing volatile matter.
questions.explanation: The key differences are the amount of air and the type of ore commonly treated.
questions.commonMistake: State the air condition clearly for each process.

questions.prompt: Why is electrolytic reduction used for extracting aluminium?
questions.answer: Aluminium is a highly reactive metal and its oxide is very stable. It cannot be reduced satisfactorily by carbon or common chemical reducing agents, so extraction is carried out by electrolytic reduction of its molten compound.
questions.explanation: High reactivity and stability of compounds necessitate electrolysis.
questions.commonMistake: Relate the method to aluminium’s position in the activity series.

questions.prompt: State two reasons for making alloys.
questions.answer: Alloys are made to improve properties such as hardness and strength, and to increase resistance to corrosion. They can also be designed to have lower melting points or other desirable characteristics for specific uses.
questions.explanation: Alloying modifies properties to suit practical applications.
questions.commonMistake: Give reasons related to properties, not just naming alloys.

questions.prompt: Describe the main steps involved in the extraction of a metal from its sulphide ore.
questions.answer: First, the ore is concentrated, often by froth flotation, to remove gangue. Next, the concentrated sulphide ore is roasted in excess air to convert it into the metal oxide, releasing sulphur dioxide. The oxide is then reduced to the metal using a suitable reducing agent such as carbon, depending on reactivity. Finally, the crude metal is refined to obtain a purer product.
questions.explanation: The sequence links ore type to appropriate conversion and reduction steps.
questions.commonMistake: Include roasting as the conversion step for sulphide ores.

questions.prompt: Explain electrolytic refining of copper, stating the electrodes, electrolyte and result.
questions.answer: In electrolytic refining, the anode is a thick block of impure copper and the cathode is a thin strip of pure copper. The electrolyte is acidified copper(II) sulphate solution. On passing current, copper from the anode dissolves as Cu2+ ions and is deposited as pure copper on the cathode. Insoluble impurities settle as anode mud, resulting in purification of copper.
questions.explanation: Selective transfer of copper yields high-purity metal at the cathode.
questions.commonMistake: Identify anode and cathode materials correctly.

questions.prompt: How does the activity series influence the method used for extraction of metals? Illustrate with one example each for high, medium and low reactivity metals.
questions.answer: Metals high in the activity series form very stable compounds and are extracted by electrolysis of molten compounds, for example aluminium from molten alumina. Moderately reactive metals form oxides that can be reduced by carbon or carbon monoxide, for example iron from haematite in a furnace. Low reactivity metals have less stable compounds and may be extracted by heating or occur native, for example mercury from cinnabar or gold in native form. Thus, increasing reactivity makes chemical reduction more difficult.
questions.explanation: The method chosen reflects the stability of the metal’s compounds.
questions.commonMistake: Give appropriate examples that match each reactivity category.

questions.prompt: A metal carbonate ore is to be processed. Suggest suitable steps to obtain the metal oxide and justify them.
questions.answer: The ore should first be concentrated to remove gangue by a suitable physical method. Then it should be calcined by heating in limited or no air. Calcination decomposes the carbonate to form the metal oxide and carbon dioxide, for example CaCO3 → CaO + CO2. This oxide can then be reduced in a later step depending on the metal’s reactivity.
questions.explanation: Calcination is appropriate for carbonate ores because heating drives off CO2.
questions.commonMistake: Do not suggest roasting in excess air as the primary step for a carbonate ore.

questions.prompt: Iron rusts in moist air but aluminium objects often resist corrosion. Explain this difference in terms of surface behaviour.
questions.answer: Iron forms porous, flaky rust in the presence of air and moisture, which does not protect the underlying metal and allows corrosion to continue. Aluminium reacts with oxygen to form a thin, tough and adherent oxide layer that covers the surface and prevents further contact with air and moisture. This protective oxide layer makes aluminium more resistant to corrosion under normal conditions.
questions.explanation: The nature of the surface layer determines whether corrosion is self-limiting.
questions.commonMistake: Mention that rust is non-protective while aluminium oxide is protective.

questions.prompt: You are given an impure sample of copper. Propose a method to obtain pure copper and explain how purity improves.
questions.answer: Use electrolytic refining. Make the impure copper the anode and a thin pure copper sheet the cathode, with acidified copper(II) sulphate as electrolyte. On passing current, copper from the anode dissolves as Cu2+ ions and deposits as pure copper on the cathode. Insoluble impurities settle as anode mud and soluble impurities remain in solution, so the cathode gradually becomes a block of pure copper.
questions.explanation: Controlled electrolytic transfer separates copper from impurities.
questions.commonMistake: State the roles of anode mud and electrolyte clearly.

questions.prompt: Why is an alloy preferred over a pure metal for making aircraft bodies or electrical heating elements in many cases? Give a reasoned answer.
questions.answer: Pure metals may be too soft, too prone to corrosion, or may lack the required strength or melting characteristics. Alloys can be engineered to provide higher strength-to-weight ratio, better corrosion resistance or suitable electrical and thermal properties. For example, alloying can make materials stronger and more durable for aircraft structures or provide appropriate resistance and stability for heating elements.
questions.explanation: Alloying tailors material properties to demanding applications.
questions.commonMistake: Relate the preference to specific property improvements, not just that alloys are mixtures.
